turns.prompt_text: I've got a clogged sink pipe and it's still there after taking the u-pipe out, the trap And it's still there after the Drano What is the next step? Isn't it some kind of auger plunger thing? Is there a tool to use that I could combine with any of my Milwaukee power tools?
turns.response_html:
You are exactly right. If the p-trap (u-bend) is clear, the blockage is further down the branch line inside the wall. The tool you are thinking of is a drum auger (commonly called a drain snake).

Since you already have Milwaukee power tools, you don't need to buy a dedicated electric plumbing machine. You can pick up a drill-adaptable drum auger at any hardware store for around $30 to $40.

Instead of a hand crank, these have a standard 1/4-inch hex shank protruding from the back of the drum. You chuck your Milwaukee drill directly onto it, and the drill does the work of spinning the cable through the clog.

⚠️ Critical Safety Note First

Because you already used Drano, the water sitting behind that clog is highly caustic. When you open the pipe to snake it, or when the snake flicks water as it spins, you risk splashing chemicals into your eyes or onto your skin. You must wear safety glasses and waterproof rubber or nitrile gloves (do not use leather or fabric gloves, as they will absorb the chemicals).

As you pull the cable back into the drum, wipe it down with a rag so it doesn't rust inside the housing.

Hitting a hard stop in the wall is incredibly common. When your snake hits a 90-degree elbow or a T-junction, it feels exactly like hitting a solid brick wall — whereas hitting the actual clog usually feels like pushing into thick mud.

If the cable refuses to turn the corner, don't just lean your body weight into it (that will just cause the cable to kink and fold over on itself). Instead, try these techniques:

1. The "Spin and Push" Method

Pull the cable back an inch or two from the hard stop. Lock the thumbscrew, start the drill on a slow forward spin, and then gently push the spinning cable forward. The rotation helps the corkscrew tip "walk" along the inside curve of the pipe rather than jamming straight into the wall.

2. The Reverse Kick

If forward spinning just grinds against the corner, switch your drill to reverse. Give it a few slow, short bursts while applying gentle forward pressure. The backwards rotation often causes the tip to jump over the internal lip of a stubborn T-junction. Note: Only do this in short bursts. Running an auger in reverse for too long can cause the cable to unspool and tangle inside the drum.

3. Pre-Bend the Tip

If you are completely stuck, pull the cable all the way out of the wall. Take a pair of pliers and put a slight 30-to-45-degree bend about an inch behind the corkscrew tip. When you feed it back in and start spinning, that angled tip acts like a radar dish — it will sweep the inside of the pipe until it naturally finds the opening of the turn and slips in.

4. Ditch the Drill (Temporarily)

Power tools are great for chewing through clogs, but they rob you of tactile feedback. If the drill isn't working, take it off. Lock the thumbscrew and manually twist the drum back and forth with your hands while applying forward pressure. You will be able to feel exactly what the tip is doing and can often finesse it past the corner better by hand. Once you drop past the elbow, you can hook the Milwaukee drill back up to finish the job.

turns.prompt_text: So some of the white pipe PVC is not unscrewing, it is stuck
turns.response_html:
Those plastic slip-joint nuts can get incredibly stubborn, especially if minerals from the water have calcified in the threads over time.

Because you are dealing with thin PVC and there is caustic Drano sitting right behind that connection, do not use power tools to force it. An impact driver or drill will instantly crack the plastic, spilling the chemical water everywhere.

Here is how to break it loose safely:

1. Upgrade Your Grip (The Towel Trick)

Before reaching for metal tools, put on your rubber or nitrile gloves (remember the Drano hazard). Grab a damp rag or one of those grippy rubber jar-opener pads and wrap it around the nut. This gives your hand significantly more torque without squeezing the pipe out of round.

2. Apply Hot Water

If the nut is seized due to dried gunk or mild calcification, heat can expand the plastic just enough to break the bond. Soak a rag in the hottest water your tap can produce (do not use a heat gun or torch, which will melt the PVC) and wrap it around the stuck nut for about 5 minutes. Try twisting it by hand again while it's still warm.

3. Use Slip-Joint Pliers (Channellocks) or a Strap Wrench

If hand pressure isn't enough, you need mechanical leverage.

Grab a pair of large adjustable slip-joint pliers (Channellocks). The trick here is to avoid squeezing too hard. If you squeeze the handles tightly, you will compress the plastic nut into an oval, which actually makes it bind tighter to the threads and can crack it. Adjust the pliers so the jaws grip the ridges of the nut without you having to squeeze the handles shut. Apply slow, steady turning pressure.

Alternatively, a rubber strap wrench is the safest mechanical tool because it applies even turning force all the way around the nut without squeezing it.

4. Cut and Replace (The Last Resort)

If you've tried heat and pliers and the nut still won't budge, it is permanently cross-threaded or fused. At this point, the safest option is to use a hacksaw to carefully cut the nut or the pipe section off.

Standard 1 ½-inch or 1 ¼-inch tubular PVC sink kits are incredibly cheap (usually under $10 at any hardware store). It is much less frustrating to simply cut the stubborn part out and replace the trap assembly than to fight a fused nut for an hour.
